title: Direct Interaction of Dengue Virus with Human Platelets Drives Membrane Remodeling, Caspase-3 Activation, and Extracellular Vesicle Release
content: Dengue virus (DENV) infection is a frequent cause of acute thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, yet underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the dynamics of platelet activation, morphological changes, apoptosis, and extracellular vesicle (EV) release in human platelets exposed to DENV-2 (MOI 0.1) for 2 h and 4 h. Washed platelets from healthy donors (n=5) exhibited marked donor-to-donor heterogeneity in CD62P and CD40L surface mobilization, with no statistically significant shifts in positivity or mean fluorescence intensity (p>0.05). Conversely, scanning electron microscopy morphometry demonstrated significant platelet spreading, showing increased equatorial diameter at 2 h and 4 h versus mock controls (p<0.0001), reaching dimensions comparable to collagen activation. Notably, DENV-2 exposure induced a marked increase in caspase-3 activation at 2 h and 4 h compared to mock and collagen conditions (p<0.001). In contrast, collagen stimulation did not elicit detectable caspase-3 activation, suggesting that DENV-2 triggers apoptotic signaling distinct from a conventional activation. Nanoparticle tracking analysis showed that total EVs abundance remained comparable across conditions (p>0.05), but DENV-2 preferentially enriched medium-sized microvesicles (150–250 nm). These findings suggest that platelet responses to DENV-2 exhibit a distinct pattern of degranulation, morphological spreading, and for caspase-3-mediated apoptotic activation, providing new insights into cellular mechanisms potentially contributing of the dengue-induced thrombocytopenia.
